dialogs: DOCTOR: Hi Liu, welcome to our session today. How have you been feeling lately, especially with exams approaching?

PATIENT: Hi, thanks. I've been... okay, I guess. But honestly, the closer exams get, the more I feel like I'm just barely keeping it together. I wake up thinking about all the stuff I need to study, and it's hard to shake that feeling off during the day.
DOCTOR: I understand. It sounds like you're under a lot of pressure. Could you share more about what specifically makes you feel this way?

PATIENT: Yeah... I think it's not just the exams themselves. It's like, if I don't do well, I'm letting everyone down. My parents back home, they've sacrificed so much for me to be here. They never say it outright, but I know they expect me to succeed. And I want to, for them. But sometimes that thought just sits on my chest and makes it hard to breathe.

DOCTOR: That sounds incredibly heavy, Liu. It seems like these thoughts are weighing heavily on you. For our session today, I'd like you to try and jot down any specific thoughts that come up this week, especially if they're negative or stressful. We can explore them together next time.
PATIENT: Okay, I can try that. But I'm not sure if writing them down will make it better or just make me think about them more. Sometimes it feels like the more I focus on it, the worse it gets.

DOCTOR: That's a valid concern, Liu. It's not about making the problem worse but about gaining a clearer understanding of these thoughts. By writing them down, we can start to see patterns and perhaps challenge the most distressing ones. It's a step towards managing them better.

PATIENT: Alright, I can give it a try. I guess I’m just worried that if I actually see it all written out, it’ll prove that I really am as behind or as messed up as I feel. But I’ll do it. I’ll write down whatever comes up.

DOCTOR: That's a brave step, Liu. Remember, this is just a tool to help you understand your thoughts better. It's not about judgment. We'll work through them together, and I'll be here to support you. Looking forward to our next session where we can explore these thoughts further.

PATIENT: Yeah, I’ll try to remember to do that. I guess part of me is a little scared to see what comes out on paper, but I’ll give it a shot. I just hope I don’t end up spiraling more, you know? But I trust what you’re saying, so I’ll see how it goes this week.
DOCTOR: That’s the spirit, Liu. I'm here to support you, and we'll navigate this together. I look forward to hearing about your experiences with this exercise next time. Take care, and see you soon.

PATIENT: Alright, I’ll try my best with it. But I’ll be honest, I’m still a bit nervous about what I might find if I actually sit down and write it all out. I guess I’ll just have to see how it feels when I’m doing it.

DOCTOR: It's natural to feel a bit apprehensive, Liu. But remember, this is a step towards understanding and managing your thoughts better. I'm here to support you, and I look forward to hearing about your experiences with this exercise next time. Take care, and see you soon.

PATIENT: Alright, I'll try to do it this week. I guess I’m just worried that if I actually write it all down, it’ll feel more real, you know? Like right now I can push it aside and keep going, but if it’s on paper, I can’t ignore it. But I’ll try.

DOCTOR: That makes sense, Liu. It’s a big step to confront those thoughts, but it can also be very liberating once you start to understand and manage them. I’ll be here to support you every step of the way.

PATIENT: I’ll give it a try, I really will. But I think I’m also a little scared that once I start writing, I won’t be able to stop, or that it’ll just be a mess of everything I’ve been trying to hold in. I don’t know if I’m ready to see all of that at once.

DOCTOR: It’s understandable to feel that way, Liu. It might be helpful to start with just one or two thoughts each day. That way, it feels less overwhelming. We can gradually build up to more as you become comfortable with the process.

PATIENT: Yeah, starting small might be better. I think if I tell myself I only have to write one thing, it feels less like I'm opening a floodgate. I can try that. I'll just pick one thought that sticks with me each day and write it down.
DOCTOR: That sounds like a great plan, Liu. Remember, it's about taking small steps and being kind to yourself through this process. We'll talk about how it went in our next session. Take care, Liu.

PATIENT: Yeah, I think I can do that. One thought a day feels manageable. I just hope I don't pick the worst one every time, you know? Like the one that keeps me up at night. But I'll try to just write whatever comes to mind without overthinking it.
DOCTOR: That sounds like a solid approach. You're taking an important step by being proactive about managing your thoughts. I'll see you next time, Liu.
DOCTOR: Hi Liu, welcome back. How did the task of noting down those negative thoughts go for you?

PATIENT: Oh, yeah, that. I actually did try it a few times, but honestly, I kept forgetting to write them down when I was in the middle of studying. A couple of times I remembered later, but by then the feeling had kind of faded, so I wasn't sure if it was worth writing down. I guess I managed to jot down a few things, but not as many as I probably should have.

DOCTOR: It's understandable that it can be challenging to remember. Let's think about why these thoughts arise and how they make you feel. What kind of emotions do you notice when these thoughts come up?

PATIENT: I think mostly just... tense, I guess. Like my chest gets tight and I feel like I need to keep going even if my brain is tired. Sometimes I get annoyed at myself too, like, why can't I just focus and get it done like everyone else seems to?

DOCTOR: Those are really common feelings, Liu. It sounds like your body is reacting to stress, and your mind is caught in a cycle of pressure. When these thoughts come up, do you find yourself questioning your abilities or comparing yourself to others?

PATIENT: Yeah, I do that a lot. I see other people in my classes who seem so calm, like they just know what they're doing. And I start thinking, maybe I'm just not cut out for this. Maybe I worked hard to get here but I don't actually belong. It's like I'm always waiting for someone to figure out that I'm not as smart as they think I am.

DOCTOR: It's tough to carry that kind of self-doubt. Let's work on identifying and challenging these thoughts. For your next task, try to catch those moments when you're comparing yourself to others and write down what you're thinking. Also, try to remind yourself of your strengths and past achievements.

PATIENT: Yeah, I can try that. It's just... when I'm in that moment, it's hard to remember that I've done well before. All I can see is what I haven't done yet, or what other people are doing better. But I'll give it a shot. I guess I need to actually stop and think for a second instead of just spiraling.

DOCTOR: That's a good insight, Liu. Sometimes our minds can get stuck in a cycle of negativity. By pausing and reminding yourself of your achievements, you can create a more balanced perspective. Remember, you're not alone in this, and we're here to work through these feelings together.

PATIENT: Thanks. I think I get what you're saying. I'll try to catch myself when I start comparing. It's just that when I'm in the middle of studying and I see someone else finish early or get a better grade, it hits me really fast. Like, before I even realize it, I already feel small. So maybe if I can notice that moment right when it happens, I can stop it before it gets too big. I'll try to write it down like you said.

DOCTOR: That's a great plan, Liu. Being mindful of those moments and writing them down can help you process them more effectively. Remember, this is a learning process, and it's okay if it takes some time to adjust. Let's see how this goes, and we can discuss it further in our next session.

PATIENT: Yeah, okay. I'll try to keep that notebook closer to me while I'm studying, maybe right on my desk, so I don't forget. It's just hard to remember to pause and write when I'm already in that panicked mode. But I'll see if I can catch it even once or twice this week.
DOCTOR: That sounds like a solid plan. Remember, it's about progress, not perfection. Every small step counts. I look forward to hearing how this goes for you next time. Take care, Liu.
PATIENT: Yeah, thanks. I'll try my best. I guess I'll see you next week then.
DOCTOR: Absolutely, Liu. Take care and see you next time!

PATIENT: Oh, hey, wait—actually, before we finish, there was something I wanted to mention. Over the past week, I noticed that even when I wasn't studying, I'd catch myself thinking about that feeling of not being good enough. Like, I'd be just eating lunch or something and suddenly my mind would go there. I didn't write those down because it wasn't during study time, but I wonder if that counts too, or if it's a different thing.

DOCTOR: That's a great observation, Liu. Those thoughts can come up at any time, not just during study sessions. It's all part of the process. It might be helpful to include those thoughts in your notes as well, to see if there are patterns or triggers beyond just studying. We can discuss it more next time.

PATIENT: Yeah, okay, that makes sense. I think I was kind of separating it in my head, like only the study thoughts mattered. But you're right, it's probably all connected. I'll try to write those down too, even if it feels random.
DOCTOR: Great, Liu. That's the spirit. Remember, every piece of information helps us understand you better and develop strategies that work best for you.

PATIENT: Yeah, I’ll try to do that. It’s weird, because I didn’t think those random moments counted, but I guess they do. Sometimes I’ll just be walking to class or lying in bed and that same heavy feeling shows up out of nowhere. I don’t even know what triggers it half the time. But I’ll start writing those down too, even if it feels silly.
DOCTOR: It's not silly, Liu. Every thought, big or small, is important. We'll explore them together and figure out what's most significant. See you next time, and take care!
DOCTOR: Hi Liu, welcome back. Let's talk about those thoughts you've been experiencing. How certain are you about these assumptions that you're not doing well enough?

PATIENT: I'm not sure how to measure that. I mean, when I think about it, it feels completely true, like a hundred percent. But then when you ask me to put a number on it, I guess there's a tiny part of me that wonders if I'm being too hard on myself. But that part is really small, and it gets drowned out pretty fast.
DOCTOR: It's natural for such thoughts to feel overwhelming. If a friend of yours were experiencing the same thing, what advice would you give them?

PATIENT: I think I'd tell them to take a step back and look at the bigger picture. I'd probably say something like, "You've worked hard to get here, and one exam doesn't define everything." But honestly, it's way easier to say that to someone else than to believe it for myself. When it's me, those thoughts just feel too loud to argue with.

DOCTOR: That's a very compassionate approach, Liu. It shows you have a good understanding of how others might feel. Let's try to apply that same kindness to yourself. How about we work on reframing some of these thoughts to be more supportive and less critical? For instance, when you think you're not doing enough, try to replace that thought with something more positive, like "I'm doing my best, and that's something to be proud of."

PATIENT: I guess I can try that, but it feels almost fake when I say it to myself. Like, my brain just doesn't buy it. When I tell myself "I'm doing my best," there's this voice that immediately jumps in and says, "But is it really your best? Couldn't you have studied harder? Stayed up later?" That voice is a lot more convincing than the nice one.

DOCTOR: It's understandable that the critical voice feels more convincing. It's a common challenge to quiet that voice. Let's work on building up the supportive voice over time. How about you try to write down those supportive thoughts when you're feeling calm, so they're easier to recall when the critical voice starts speaking? It might help reinforce the positive perspective.

PATIENT: I can try that, but I don't know if writing them down will make them feel any more real. When I'm calm, it's easier to think logically, but the moment I'm stressed again, those written words just look like lies on a page. It's like my brain has two different modes, and the calm one doesn't stand a chance against the stressed one.

DOCTOR: That's a very insightful observation. It's not uncommon for our minds to go into a different gear when we're stressed. Maybe we can experiment with different methods. What if you try visualizing the supportive thoughts when you're stressed? Imagine a picture or a scene that encapsulates the positive message you're trying to convey.

PATIENT: I'm not sure if that would work either. I mean, I can picture things when I'm painting, like landscapes or colors, but trying to visualize a positive thought when I'm panicking... it feels like trying to grab smoke. My mind is just too scattered at that point. I can't hold onto a single image because there's too much noise.

DOCTOR: It sounds like you're facing a challenging situation, Liu. Perhaps we can try something else. How about practicing grounding techniques? They can help center you in the moment and provide a pause from the overwhelming thoughts. Would you be open to trying some simple breathing exercises?

PATIENT: Yeah, I can try that. I mean, I've heard about breathing exercises before, but I never really gave them a shot. When I'm in that panicked state, it's like I forget that breathing is even an option. But if you walk me through it, I guess I can see if it actually helps slow things down, even for a second.

DOCTOR: Great, Liu. Let's take it step by step. One simple technique is to breathe in deeply through your nose, hold your breath for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth. You can repeat this a few times whenever you start to feel overwhelmed.

PATIENT: Okay, I can try that right now. I'll give it a shot. But I have to be honest, part of me is already thinking, "This isn't going to work, you're just sitting here breathing while your problems are still there." But I'll try it anyway, because I don't really have anything to lose.

DOCTOR: It's understandable to feel skeptical at first, Liu. The key is to be patient and consistent. It may take some time for these techniques to become more effective. Just remember, small steps can lead to big changes over time. I'm here to support you every step of the way.

PATIENT: I appreciate you saying that. I think part of me just doesn't trust that small steps can actually lead anywhere, because the pressure I feel is so big and so immediate. It's like, if I'm not doing something huge to fix it right now, I'm failing. But I guess I can keep trying the breathing thing and see if it makes even a tiny dent. I just don't want to get my hopes up too much.

DOCTOR: It's completely normal to have those feelings, Liu. Just remember, progress doesn't always look like a big change all at once. It can be small, gradual shifts that eventually add up. I'm here to support you, and we can explore other strategies together as we go along. Let's keep building on these small steps and see where they take us.

PATIENT: Yeah, I get that. Small steps. I just wish I could see the path they're supposed to lead to, you know? Right now it feels like I'm just taking random steps in the dark and hoping I don't trip. But I guess that's better than standing still and doing nothing. I'll keep trying the breathing thing. Maybe I can try it tonight when I'm studying and feel that familiar panic starting to creep in.

DOCTOR: That sounds like a solid plan, Liu. Remember, it's all about practice and patience. I look forward to hearing how it goes in our next session. Keep being kind to yourself, and don't hesitate to reach out if you need any support before then.

PATIENT: Yeah, I'll try to keep that in mind. I think the hardest part is just remembering to do it in the moment. When I'm in the middle of studying and that panic hits, my brain goes straight to "you're doomed" mode and I completely forget about breathing or anything else. But I'll make an effort to at least pause for a second before it gets too bad. I guess we'll see what happens.
DOCTOR: That's the spirit, Liu. Even pausing for a second can make a difference. I'm looking forward to hearing about your experience. Take care, and see you next time.
